title: Parade's End
description: The greatest English novel of the First World War: Tietjens, the trenches and the end of the old England, in four volumes. It is a prose fiction work of 1924 by Ford Madox Ford; it belongs to The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England and it is catalogued here under War Memoir and the Autobiographical Testimony; Novel of Consciousness and the Stream of Mind and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The tetralogy — Some Do Not… (1924), No More Parades (1925), A Man Could Stand Up (1926) and The Last Post (1928) — follows Christopher Tietjens through the collapse of his marriage, his service on the Western Front, his love for Valentine Wannop, and his post-war life in the Sussex countryside, and ends with the birth of his child and the death of his brother Mark.
narrative_structure: Four volumes: two pre-war and war, two war and post-war. It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel organised by the movement of consciousness rather than by chronology: long unbroken passages of thought, time-shifts and repetitions, with the external action reported from inside a single mind.
principal_characters: Christopher Tietjens; Sylvia Tietjens; Valentine Wannop; Mark Tietjens; Marie Léonie; General Campion
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the interior: long unbroken periods, free indirect discourse, the time-shift and the associative leap, with the punctuation and syntax following the movement of the mind rather than the order of events. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The author's characteristic manner is the impressionist method: the scene rendered as it strikes a mind, in broken chronology, with the narrator's hesitations left in.
historical_context: The First World War and the Edwardian world it destroyed, from the golf links of Rye to the mud of the Somme and the peace of a Sussex farm. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1928 and first published in 1924 and the corpus places it within The Edwardian Country House and the Condition of England; Trench Poetry and the Literature of the First World War, it is catalogued under war memoir and the autobiographical testimony; novel of consciousness and the stream of mind.
literary_significance: Parade's End is the greatest English novel of the First World War and the finest study of the transition from Edwardian to modern England: its technical innovation, its portrait of Tietjens as the last gentleman and its movement from the war to the peace made it a permanent work.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Ford Hermann Hueffer. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: The four novels were published separately: Some Do Not... (John Lane, April 1924), No More Parades (Duckworth, March 1925), A Man Could Stand Up-- (Duckworth, January 1926) and The Last Post (Duckworth, March 1928); the tetralogy was issued in one volume as Parade's End by Knopf in New York in 1950. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Garden Party and Other Stories
description: Mansfield's finest collection: the garden party, the doll's house, the fly and the last stories of loss. It is a prose fiction work of 1922 by Katherine Mansfield; it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.

narrative_structure: Fifteen stories, several set in the same New Zealand world. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine.
principal_characters: Laura Sheridan; the workmen; Kezia Burnell; the boss; the fly
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the story without a plot: a moment of perception, a family scene, a shift of light.
historical_context: The New Zealand of Mansfield's childhood and the England of the war and after, written while she was dying of tuberculosis. The record dates the work as composed between 1921 and 1922 and first published in 1922 and it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale.
literary_significance: The Garden Party is the summit of Mansfield's art and one of the finest short-story collections in English: 'At the Bay' and 'The Garden Party' changed the form, and the collection's exact surface with its hidden grief is the model for the modern story.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Kathleen Mansfield Beauchamp. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

title: A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle
alternative_titles: Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle
description: The greatest long poem in Scots: a drunk man's night on a hillside with a thistle, and the whole condition of Scotland. It is a verse work of 1926 by Hugh MacDiarmid; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Modernist Long Poem and the Mythical Method; Dialect Poem and Vernacular Performance and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The speaker, drunk, lies on a hillside beside a thistle and holds a night-long argument with it: about Scotland, Calvinism, the Scots language, love, drink, the industrial city, communism, the universe and his own soul, in a sequence of lyric passages and dramatic monologues that moves between Scots and English.
narrative_structure: A night-long sequence of lyric and dramatic passages in Scots and English. A long poem built as a sequence of fragments in several voices, ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative sequence. A collection of poems written to be performed, each a separate monologue or song in the spoken dialect.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse in the modernist long poem: the polyphonic sequence of fragments in free verse and in borrowed metres, quotation and allusion doing the work of connective argument, the whole ordered by a mythic or symbolic pattern rather than by narrative. The author's characteristic manner is the synthetic Scots lyric with its dictionary richness.
historical_context: The Scotland of the 1920s: the industrial depression, the loss of the Scots language, the Calvinist inheritance, and the nationalist revival of the Scottish Renaissance. The record dates the work as composed between 1925 and 1926 and first published in 1926 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under modernist long poem and the mythical method; dialect poem and vernacular performance.
literary_significance: A Drunk Man Looks at the Thistle is the greatest long poem in Scots and the founding work of the Scottish Renaissance: it restored Scots as a modern literary language, made the condition of Scotland the subject of a great poem, and is one of the permanent long poems of the century.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Christopher Murray Grieve. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1926, as long poem, by Hugh MacDiarmid. Composed between 1925 and 1926. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Sunset Song
description: The finest Scottish novel of the century: Chris Guthrie, the Mearns farming country, and the destruction of a world by war and the machine. It is a prose fiction work of 1932 by Lewis Grassic Gibbon; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Chris Guthrie grows up on a croft in the Mearns, is torn between her mother's Scots and her father's English, watches her family break up and her father die, marries the farmer Ewan Tavendale, and loses him to the First World War. The novel ends with the village dead of the war, the farms sold, and Chris leaving for the city.
narrative_structure: Four parts (Prelude, The Song, The Woman, Epilude) with choric openings. A continuous prose narrative in chapters, the action carried in sequence from the opening situation to the closing resolution.
principal_characters: Chris Guthrie; Jean Guthrie; John Guthrie; Ewan Tavendale; Chae Strachan; Long Rob
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction: the continuous chaptered narrative carries description, dialogue and reflection. The author's characteristic manner is the Scots-inflected English narrative that shifts register with the characters' consciousness.
historical_context: The farming country of the Mearns between 1911 and 1919, the First World War, and the agricultural depression that emptied the land. The record dates the work as composed between 1931 and 1932 and first published in 1932 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle.
literary_significance: Sunset Song is the finest Scottish novel of the century and one of the great novels of rural dispossession in English: its Scots-inflected prose, its choric parish voice and its elegy for a destroyed world made it a permanent classic.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James Leslie Mitchell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1932, as novel (first of a scots quair), by Lewis Grassic Gibbon. Composed between 1931 and 1932. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: A Scots Quair
description: The great Scottish trilogy: the land, the town and the city in one woman's life, and the passage of Scotland into the modern world. It is a prose fiction work of 1932 by Lewis Grassic Gibbon; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Provincial Novel and the British Rural Chronicle; Condition-of-England Novel and the Edwardian Social Panorama and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The trilogy — Sunset Song (1932), Cloud Howe (1933) and Grey Granite (1934) — follows Chris Guthrie from the Mearns croft through her marriage to a minister in the small town of Segget and her son Ewan's life as a communist agitator in the industrial city of Duncairn.
narrative_structure: Three volumes, each with its own setting and its choric openings. It was issued in volumes, the division marked by the pause in the action. A novel in chapters of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, the argument carried by contrast between scenes.
principal_characters: Chris Guthrie; Ewan Tavendale; Robert Colquohoun; Ewan Colquohoun; Ellen Johns
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the social panorama: the long sentence of survey, the household and the institution described as types of the whole society, and the argument carried by contrast between scenes rather than by authorial comment. The work was issued in volumes, the division marked in the text. The work is a trilogy, its three parts complete in themselves and continuous in their subject. The author's characteristic manner is the Scots-inflected English narrative that shifts register with the characters' consciousness.
historical_context: Scotland from 1911 to the Depression of the 1930s: the farming Mearns, the small town, and the industrial city. The record dates the work as composed between 1931 and 1934 and first published in 1932 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under provincial novel and the british rural chronicle; condition-of-england novel and the edwardian social panorama.
literary_significance: A Scots Quair is the most complete account in fiction of Scotland's passage from the land to the city in a single generation: its three volumes, its Scots prose and its historical sweep made it the central work of the Scottish Renaissance.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James Leslie Mitchell. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1932, as novel trilogy (three volumes, 1932–34), by Lewis Grassic Gibbon. Composed between 1931 and 1934. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Story and the Fable
description: One of the finest Scottish autobiographies: Orkney, the ruined family in Glasgow, and the myth of Eden. It is a prose work of 1940 by Edwin Muir; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Autobiography and the Modern Memoir; Biography and the Modern Life.
plot_or_argument: Muir recounts his Orkney childhood on a farm, the family's move to Glasgow and its destruction by poverty and illness, his work in a bone factory and an office, and the slow discovery of his vocation — and interprets it through the myth of the fall and the lost Eden that shapes his poetry.
narrative_structure: Autobiographical chapters interspersed with the mythic interpretation. An autobiography in chapters, the formative scenes set piece by set piece, with letters and diaries quoted at the turning points. A documented life in chapters, told with the scene and dialogue of the novelist and the quotation from the papers.
principal_characters: Edwin Muir; his family; Orkney; Glasgow
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of autobiography: the first-person narrative of the life, the set-piece of the formative scene, the quotation from letters and diaries, and the reflection on the formation of a self. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, mythic, unnervingly simple lyric.
historical_context: The Orkney islands and the Glasgow slums of the 1890s and 1900s, the First World War, and the literary London of the 1920s. The record dates the work as composed between 1939 and 1940 and first published in 1940 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under autobiography and the modern memoir; biography and the modern life.
literary_significance: The Story and the Fable is one of the great Scottish autobiographies and the key to Muir's poetry: its account of the fall from Orkney into Glasgow made the myth of Eden the centre of his work, and it is one of the finest autobiographies of the period.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1940, as autobiography, by Edwin Muir. Composed between 1939 and 1940. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: The Narrow Place
description: Muir's finest collection: the mythic lyric of Eden, the journey and the labyrinth. It is a verse work of 1943 by Edwin Muir; it belongs to The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival and it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Combat', 'The Narrow Place', 'The River', 'The Return' and the poems of the journey and the dream that made Muir's reputation, in the plain mythic manner of his middle period.
narrative_structure: A collection of lyrics and short sequences. A collection of separate poems rather than a continuous narrative; the pieces stand alone and are commonly read individually.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, mythic, unnervingly simple lyric.
historical_context: The Scotland of Muir's memory, the Second World War, and the mythic imagination of his middle years. The record dates the work as composed between 1941 and 1943 and first published in 1943 and the corpus places it within The Scottish Renaissance and the Vernacular Revival, it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom.

attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1943, as poetry collection, by Edwin Muir. Composed between 1941 and 1943. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Three Lives
description: Stein's first major work: three working-class women of Baltimore, and a prose that dismantles the nineteenth-century sentence. It is a prose fiction work of 1909 by Gertrude Stein; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The three lives — 'The Good Anna', 'Melanctha' and 'The Gentle Lena' — are those of a German servant, a Black woman and a German immigrant girl in the small town of Bridgepoint, told in a prose of repetition, present tense and simple declarative sentences that refuses the conventions of the Victorian novel.
narrative_structure: Three separate lives, each in its own section, in a prose of repetition and continuous present.
principal_characters: Anna; Melanctha Herbert; Lena; Jeff Campbell; Dr Jeff Campbell
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the continuous present and the deliberate repetition.
historical_context: The Baltimore of Stein's childhood, the working-class immigrant and Black communities, and the new psychology of William James that Stein had studied at Radcliffe. The record dates the work as composed between 1905 and 1908 and first published in 1909 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; modern short story and the magazine tale.
literary_significance: Three Lives is the first work of literary modernism in English by an American and the foundation of Stein's experimental prose: its repetition, its present tense and its refusal of plot made it the model for Hemingway's sentences and for a whole century of American prose.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Grafton Press of New York in December 1909, at the author's own expense. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Tender Buttons
description: The most radical book of the period: objects, food and rooms, in a prose that abolishes the noun's ordinary work. It is a verse work of 1914 by Gertrude Stein; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under Modernist Lyric and the New Idiom and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The three sections — 'Objects', 'Food' and 'Rooms' — are sequences of short prose portraits of a carafe, a chair, a plate, a room, in which Stein repeats and displaces words until the object appears as a pattern of language rather than a description.
narrative_structure: Three sections of short prose pieces, arranged as a cubist still life. A single poem, read as one continuous whole from its opening to its close.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse: the line and stanza follow the conventions of the genre, and the poem is written to be read aloud. The author's characteristic manner is the continuous present and the deliberate repetition.
historical_context: The Paris of the 1910s, the Cubist painting of Picasso and Braque that Stein was collecting, and the new avant-garde little magazines. The record dates the work as composed between 1912 and 1913 and first published in 1914 and the corpus places it within The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel, it is catalogued under modernist lyric and the new idiom.
literary_significance: Tender Buttons is the most radical book of the period and the founding text of literary Cubism: it dissolved the descriptive sentence into pattern and repetition, and it remains the extreme limit of what prose poetry can do.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Claire Marie of New York in October 1914 in an edition of some 500 copies. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas
description: The most entertaining memoir of the period: Stein's own life told in the voice of her companion, and the whole Paris avant-garde. It is a prose work of 1933 by Gertrude Stein; it belongs to The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel and it is catalogued here under Biography and the Modern Life; Autobiography and the Modern Memoir and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Stein writes her own autobiography in the first person of Alice B. Toklas: the San Francisco childhood, the Paris apartment at 27 rue de Fleurus, the sittings for Picasso, the Saturday evenings with Matisse, Apollinaire, Hemingway, Fitzgerald and the whole of the avant-garde, the war years and the American lecture tour.
narrative_structure: A chronological memoir in the voice of Alice B. Toklas, with an epilogue. A documented life in chapters, told with the scene and dialogue of the novelist and the quotation from the papers. An autobiography in chapters, the formative scenes set piece by set piece, with letters and diaries quoted at the turning points.
principal_characters: Gertrude Stein; Alice B. Toklas; Pablo Picasso; Henri Matisse; Ernest Hemingway; F. Scott Fitzgerald; Guillaume Apollinaire
literary_form: Memoir (written as if by Alice B. Toklas)
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the new biography: the documented life told with the novelist's scene and dialogue, the quotation from letters and papers, and the psychological interpretation offered as inference rather than as assertion. The author's characteristic manner is the continuous present and the deliberate repetition.
historical_context: The Paris of 1903–32, the avant-garde art world, the First World War, and the American discovery of modernism in the 1930s. The record dates the work as composed in 1932 and first published in 1933 and the corpus places it within The Lost Generation and the Expatriate Novel, it is catalogued under biography and the modern life; autobiography and the modern memoir.
literary_significance: The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas is the most entertaining memoir of the period and a landmark of modernist self-fashioning: it made Stein a best-seller at fifty-nine and remains the most vivid record of the Paris avant-garde.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1933, as memoir (written as if by alice b. toklas), by Gertrude Stein. Composed in 1932. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Winesburg, Ohio
description: The founding book of the modern American short story: the small town as a place of hidden loneliness. It is a prose fiction work of 1919 by Sherwood Anderson; it belongs to American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The stories follow George Willard, a young reporter on the Winesburg Eagle, through the town's inhabitants — the 'grotesques' whose lives have been twisted by an untold truth — and end with George's departure for the city.
narrative_structure: Twenty-two linked stories with an introduction and a closing departure. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine. A novel in chapters inside one region, the seasons, the trades and the dialect carrying the plot.
principal_characters: George Willard; Wing Biddlebaum; Doctor Reefy; Elizabeth Willard; Kate Swift; Alice Hindman
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The author's characteristic manner is the plain, bare, repetitive sentence.
historical_context: The small town of Clyde, Ohio, of Anderson's childhood, and the American small town at the moment of industrialisation. The record dates the work as composed between 1915 and 1919 and first published in 1919 and the corpus places it within American Modernism and the Objectivist Lyric, it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale; regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance.
literary_significance: Winesburg, Ohio is the founding book of the modern American short story: it made the small town a place of hidden lives, invented the linked story cycle as an American form, and its influence runs through Hemingway, Faulkner and Carver.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

title: The Weary Blues
description: The first book of the Harlem Renaissance to make the blues a literary form: 'The Weary Blues', 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers'. It is a verse work of 1926 by Langston Hughes; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'The Weary Blues', 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers', 'Mother to Son', 'Dream Variation', 'The South' and the poems of Harlem, the cabaret and the Black South, written in the rhythms of the blues and jazz.
narrative_structure: A collection of blues poems, lyrics and songs. A collection of lyrics in several forms, from the sonnet to the blues stanza, ordered as a continuous statement of the race's experience.
principal_characters: the blues pianist ('The Weary Blues'); the mother ('Mother to Son'); the speaker of 'The Negro Speaks of Rivers'
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse of the New Negro lyric: the blues and jazz cadence, the sermon's rising repetition, the sonnet and the ballad form turned to racial subject-matter, and the vernacular idiom used as a literary language. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the blues stanza and the jazz line.
historical_context: Harlem in the 1920s, the Great Migration, the blues of Bessie Smith and the cabarets of Lenox Avenue. The record dates the work as composed between 1921 and 1926 and first published in 1926 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under new negro lyric and the harlem renaissance poem.

attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James Mercer Langston Hughes. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.

title: The Ways of White Folks
description: Hughes's finest prose: fourteen stories of the encounters between Black and white America. It is a prose fiction work of 1934 by Langston Hughes; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: The stories — 'Cora Unashamed', 'Slave on the Block', 'Home', 'The Blues I'm Playing', 'Father and Son', 'Red-Headed Baby' — dramatise the encounters of Black servants, artists, musicians and sons with the white world, in a prose of great economy and controlled anger.
narrative_structure: Fourteen stories in varied settings, from the small town to Harlem and Paris. A short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular standing for the whole, and a turned or withheld ending, in the compass of a magazine.
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the short story: a single compressed situation, the exact particular that stands for the whole, the turned or withheld ending, and a length set by the magazine's page. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the blues stanza and the jazz line.
historical_context: The America of the early 1930s, the Harlem Renaissance's aftermath, and the encounters of race in the North and the South. The record dates the work as composed between 1932 and 1934 and first published in 1934 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under modern short story and the magazine tale.

attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as James Mercer Langston Hughes. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Alfred A. Knopf in New York in September 1934, collecting fourteen stories. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Their Eyes Were Watching God
description: The finest novel of the Harlem Renaissance: Janie Crawford's three marriages, and a Black woman's voice at the centre of American fiction. It is a prose fiction work of 1937 by Zora Neale Hurston; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance; Novel of Development and the Growth Story and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Janie Crawford, raised by her grandmother in West Florida, is married off at sixteen to an old farmer, then runs away with the ambitious Joe Starks to Eatonville, becomes the mayor's wife, and after his death falls in love with the young gambler Tea Cake. They go to the Everglades, are caught in the hurricane, and Tea Cake is bitten by a rabid dog and killed by Janie in self-defence; she returns to Eatonville alone.
narrative_structure: A framed narrative: Janie tells her story to Pheoby on her return to Eatonville. A novel in chapters inside one region, the seasons, the trades and the dialect carrying the plot. A novel in chapters grouped by the stages of a life, from childhood through the education and the first disappointments to the settlement of the adult.
principal_characters: Janie Crawford; Tea Cake; Joe Starks; Logan Killicks; Nanny; Pheoby Watson
literary_form: Novel; regional novel, first issued in 1937
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose fiction of place: the dialect dialogue and the transcribed local speech, the landscape carried in exact seasonal detail, and the plot set inside the customs, economy and geography of one region. The author's characteristic manner is free indirect style that renders Black Southern speech without condescension.
historical_context: The Black towns of Florida, Eatonville, the Everglades and the migrant labour camps of the 1920s and 1930s, and the folklore that Hurston had collected as an anthropologist. The record dates the work as composed in 1936 and first published in 1937 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro; The Southern Renaissance and the American Regional Novel, it is catalogued under regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance; novel of development and the growth story.
literary_significance: Their Eyes Were Watching God is the finest novel of the Harlem Renaissance and one of the great American novels of the century: its free indirect rendering of Black Southern speech, its portrait of a woman's self-making and its hurricane ending made it a permanent classic, recovered by Alice Walker in the 1970s and now central to the canon.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Zora Hurston. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1937, as novel, by Zora Neale Hurston. Composed in 1936. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Mules and Men
description: The great record of Black Southern folklore: the lying sessions, the work songs and the Hoodoo of Florida and New Orleans. It is a prose work of 1935 by Zora Neale Hurston; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Documentary Prose and the Reportage Book; Modern Short Story and the Magazine Tale and the record grades it as major canon and its author standing in the first rank of this corpus.
plot_or_argument: Hurston records the folklore she collected in Eatonville, Polk County and New Orleans: the 'lying' sessions, the animal tales of Brer Rabbit and Sis Cat, the work songs, the sermons, the conjure and the Hoodoo doctors, in the voices of the men and women who told them.
narrative_structure: Two parts (Florida and New Orleans), with the folk tales transcribed in dialect. A book of reportage in scenes, each scene observed and transcribed, the argument carried by the sequence rather than by commentary.
principal_characters: Hurston herself; the storytellers of Eatonville and Polk County
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of reportage: the observed scene rendered in the present tense or the immediate past, the transcribed speech of the witness, the document quoted in full, and the argument carried by the sequence of scenes. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is free indirect style that renders Black Southern speech without condescension.
historical_context: The Black rural South of the 1920s, the turpentine camps and the sawmills, and the Hoodoo tradition of New Orleans. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1935 and first published in 1935 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under documentary prose and the reportage book; modern short story and the magazine tale.
literary_significance: Mules and Men is the greatest record of Black Southern folklore and the founding text of African American anthropology: its transcription of the voices of the rural Black South preserved a culture that was disappearing, and it made Hurston the first Black woman to publish a book of anthropology.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Zora Hurston. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: First published in 1935, as folklore collection, by Zora Neale Hurston. Composed between 1927 and 1935. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Harlem Shadows
description: The first substantial book of verse of the Harlem Renaissance: the protest sonnet, the Jamaican dialect poem and Harlem. It is a verse work of 1922 by Claude McKay; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'If We Must Die', 'The Lynching', 'America', 'The Harlem Dancer', 'Tropics in New York' and the Jamaican dialect poems — the first body of West Indian verse in English.
narrative_structure: A collection of sonnets, lyrics and dialect poems. A collection of lyrics in several forms, from the sonnet to the blues stanza, ordered as a continuous statement of the race's experience.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse of the New Negro lyric: the blues and jazz cadence, the sermon's rising repetition, the sonnet and the ballad form turned to racial subject-matter, and the vernacular idiom used as a literary language. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the sonnet and the ballad used for protest.
historical_context: Harlem in the 1920s, the Red Summer of 1919, and the Jamaica of McKay's childhood. The record dates the work as composed between 1917 and 1922 and first published in 1922 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under new negro lyric and the harlem renaissance poem.
literary_significance: Harlem Shadows is the first substantial book of verse of the Harlem Renaissance and the collection that made the protest sonnet a modern form: 'If We Must Die' became an international anthem, and the Jamaican dialect poems founded West Indian literature in English.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Festus Claudius McKay. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Harcourt, Brace in New York in October 1922 with an introduction by Max Eastman; the collection gathers the poems printed in The Liberator, The Masses and elsewhere between 1917 and 1922. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Home to Harlem
description: The first best-selling Black novel of the decade: Jake Brown's Harlem, the cabarets and the return from the war. It is a prose fiction work of 1928 by Claude McKay; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Jazz-Age Novel and the Expatriate Romance; Regional Novel and the American Local-Colour Inheritance.
plot_or_argument: Jake Brown, a Black soldier who has deserted from the army in France, returns to Harlem and lives through its cabarets, rent parties and love affairs, and goes looking for his friend Ray, a Haitian intellectual, in a novel of the Black migrant city.
narrative_structure: Three parts following Jake through Harlem, the railroad and the search for Ray. A novel in chapters of the pleasure and the retrospect, the party scene and the elegiac judgement held in the same short paragraphs. A novel in chapters inside one region, the seasons, the trades and the dialect carrying the plot.
principal_characters: Jake Brown; Ray; Felice; Zeddy; Agatha
literary_form: Novel; jazz-age novel, first issued in 1928
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of the jazz age: the compressed lyrical sentence, the transcribed party dialogue and the idiom of the period, with the elegiac retrospect imposed on the scene of pleasure. The author's characteristic manner is the sonnet and the ballad used for protest.
historical_context: Harlem in the 1920s, the Great Migration, the war, and the cabaret culture of Lenox Avenue. The record dates the work as composed between 1927 and 1928 and first published in 1928 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under jazz-age novel and the expatriate romance; regional novel and the american local-colour inheritance.
literary_significance: Home to Harlem was the first best-selling novel by a Black writer of the decade and the first to make Harlem's pleasure economy a literary subject: it was attacked by Du Bois for its 'licentiousness' and defended by Hughes, and the quarrel defined the Harlem Renaissance.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Festus Claudius McKay. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as secondary canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Harper and Brothers in New York in August 1928, the first novel of the Harlem Renaissance to reach a wide audience. The record grades the work as secondary canon.

title: Color
description: The most formally accomplished first book of the Harlem Renaissance: 'Yet Do I Marvel', 'Heritage' and the English lyric. It is a verse work of 1925 by Countee Cullen; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: The collection contains 'Yet Do I Marvel', 'Heritage', 'Incident', 'Tableau', 'From the Dark Tower' and the love lyrics that made Cullen the movement's most elegant poet.
narrative_structure: A collection of sonnets, lyrics and quatrains. A collection of lyrics in several forms, from the sonnet to the blues stanza, ordered as a continuous statement of the race's experience.
principal_characters: the child of 'Incident'; Simon the Cyrenian ('Simon the Cyrenian Speaks'); the black and white lovers of 'Tableau'
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse of the New Negro lyric: the blues and jazz cadence, the sermon's rising repetition, the sonnet and the ballad form turned to racial subject-matter, and the vernacular idiom used as a literary language. The work is a collection of separate pieces in the author's or editor's order. The author's characteristic manner is the strict English lyric — the sonnet, the ballad, the quatrain and the rhymed octave.
historical_context: Harlem and New York in the 1920s, the Black church and the English lyric tradition. The record dates the work as composed between 1923 and 1925 and first published in 1925 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under new negro lyric and the harlem renaissance poem.
literary_significance: Color is the most formally accomplished first book of the Harlem Renaissance: its English lyric grace and its poems of the colour line made Cullen the movement's counterweight to Hughes, and 'Yet Do I Marvel' and 'Heritage' are permanent poems.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Countee LeRoy Porter. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Alfred A. Knopf in New York in October 1925, the first collection of poems by the author, who was twenty-two. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Caroling Dusk
description: The defining anthology of the Harlem Renaissance: thirty-eight Black poets, from Dunbar to the young writers of the 1920s. It is a verse work of 1927 by Countee Cullen; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem; Critical Essay and the Modern Review and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Cullen's anthology gathers thirty-eight African American poets — Paul Laurence Dunbar, James Weldon Johnson, Claude McKay, Langston Hughes, Jean Toomer, Arna Bontemps, Georgia Douglas Johnson, Angelina Weld Grimké and others — with a preface defending the use of the inherited English forms.
narrative_structure: An anthology of thirty-eight poets with biographical notes. A collection of lyrics in several forms, from the sonnet to the blues stanza, ordered as a continuous statement of the race's experience.
meter_and_prosody: Verse. Verse of the New Negro lyric: the blues and jazz cadence, the sermon's rising repetition, the sonnet and the ballad form turned to racial subject-matter, and the vernacular idiom used as a literary language. The work is an anthology, the pieces ordered by the editor. The author's characteristic manner is the strict English lyric — the sonnet, the ballad, the quatrain and the rhymed octave.
historical_context: The Harlem Renaissance of 1925–27 and the debate over whether Black poetry should use the folk tradition or the English lyric. The record dates the work as composed between 1926 and 1927 and first published in 1927 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under new negro lyric and the harlem renaissance poem; critical essay and the modern review.
literary_significance: Caroling Dusk is the defining anthology of the Harlem Renaissance and the book that fixed its canon: Cullen's preface made the case for the English tradition against Hughes's folk programme, and the anthology remains the essential collection of the movement's poetry.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Countee LeRoy Porter. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Harper and Brothers in New York in October 1927, the anthology of Negro verse edited by the author. The record grades the work as major canon.

title: Cane
description: The most formally radical book of the Harlem Renaissance: a collage of the Black South and the urban North. It is a prose fiction work of 1923 by Jean Toomer; it belongs to The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro and it is catalogued here under Experimental Novel and the Modernist Form; New Negro Lyric and the Harlem Renaissance Poem and the record grades it as major canon.
plot_or_argument: Cane moves from the Georgia cane fields — 'Karintha', 'Fern', 'Esther', 'Blood-Burning Moon' — through the poems and prose of the migration north to Washington and Chicago, and ends with 'Kabnis', a play of a Northern Black teacher in the South.
narrative_structure: Three parts: the Georgia South, the urban North, and the play 'Kabnis'. A novel of experiment: broken chronology, several narrators, parody of received styles and typographical play, the parts held together by pattern rather than by plot.
principal_characters: Karintha; Fern; Esther; Kabnis; Lewis; Bona; Paul
meter_and_prosody: Prose. Prose of experiment: broken chronology, multiple narrators, parody of received styles, typographical play and the deliberate difficulty of a text that refuses the continuous realistic sentence. The author's characteristic manner is the collage of genres (story, poem, drama) in a single book.
historical_context: Sparta, Georgia, where Toomer taught in 1921, and the Black migration to Washington and Chicago; the Harlem Renaissance and the new modernist art. The record dates the work as composed between 1922 and 1923 and first published in 1923 and the corpus places it within The Harlem Renaissance and the New Negro, it is catalogued under experimental novel and the modernist form; new negro lyric and the harlem renaissance poem.
literary_significance: Cane is the most formally radical book of the Harlem Renaissance and one of the great American modernist texts: its collage of story, poem and drama, its lyric prose and its structure from South to North made it the only major book of the movement as formally advanced as Ulysses or The Waste Land.
attribution_notes: Attribution is secure: the work was published under the author's name, also recorded as Nathan Pinchback Toomer. No competing attribution or spurious edition is recorded for this title. The work is catalogued here as major canon.
bibliographical_notes: Published by Boni and Liveright in New York in October 1923 in an edition of some 500 copies; the author's refusal of the publisher's offer to print it as a novel of the Negro is recorded in the correspondence. The record grades the work as major canon.
